data.title: Insert Interval
data.summary:
Input: A list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by their start times, and a new interval.
Output: The list of intervals after the new interval is inserted, merging overlapping intervals if necessary.
Rules: The output list must remain sorted by start times and have no overlapping intervals.
constraints: intervals is sorted by start_i in ascending order

data.key_insight: Since the intervals are already sorted by start time, we can iterate through the existing intervals and divide them into three phases: those that end before the new interval starts (belonging to the left), those that overlap with the new interval (which need to be merged), and those that start after the new interval ends (belonging to the right).

steps.title: Add Intervals Before New Interval
steps.detail: Iterate through the existing intervals. Append any interval that ends strictly before the new interval starts to the result list.

steps.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
steps.detail: While there are still intervals and they overlap with the new interval (i.e., the existing interval starts at or before the new interval ends), merge them by updating the new interval's start to the minimum of both starts and its end to the maximum of both ends.

steps.title: Add the Merged New Interval
steps.detail: Once all overlapping intervals are processed, append the updated new interval to the result list.

steps.title: Add Remaining Intervals
steps.detail: Append all remaining intervals that start after the new interval's end to the result list.

data.code:
class Solution:
    def insert(self, intervals: List[List[int]], newInterval: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []
        i = 0
        n = len(intervals)
        
        while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1
            
        while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
            newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
            newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
            i += 1
            
        result.append(newInterval)
        
        while i < n:
            result.append(intervals[i])
            i += 1
            
        return result

data.pattern_summary: Iterate through a sorted collection once, processing elements sequentially to build the result without unnecessary repetitions.

pattern_options.name: Linear scan
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We pass through the sorted intervals once to determine where the new interval fits and how to merge it.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps are for O(1) key-value retrieval, but here we need to maintain sequential order and ranges.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. The input is a single list of intervals rather than two independent sequences to compare.

pattern_options.name: Depth-first search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. This is not a graph or tree traversal problem.

signals.hint: Implies we can process elements in order without needing a full re-sort of everything if we handle it carefully.

data.brute_force_idea: Append the new interval to the list, sort all intervals by start time, and then iterate through to merge any overlapping pairs.
data.brute_force_why: The sorting step dominates the runtime complexity.
data.bottleneck: The direct approach is already optimal because every interval must be inspected at least once to determine its relation to the new interval, resulting in a lower bound of O(n) time.
bottleneck_hints: Consider whether you can skip looking at any intervals entirely.
Think about how many elements you must touch to ensure no overlaps are missed.
Since every interval might potentially overlap with the new interval, you must inspect each one.

data.overview: The algorithm inserts a new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals by dividing the process into three phases: adding intervals that come completely before the new interval, merging all overlapping intervals into the new interval, and adding the remaining intervals that come after.
data.intuition: Imagine sliding a card into a sorted deck of cards on a table. First, you skip past all cards that sit entirely to the left of your new card. Then, you scoop up and combine all cards that touch or overlap with your new card. Finally, you place down your merged card and slide in all the remaining cards on the right.

data.insight: The brute force approach wastes time by blindly appending the new interval and sorting the entire list from scratch, ignoring the fact that the original list is already sorted. The optimized solution exploits this existing order by dividing the array into three distinct phases: intervals before the merge zone, intervals that overlap with the new interval, and intervals after the merge zone. By scanning through the array once and handling each interval based on its position relative to the new interval, we eliminate the need for sorting entirely.

derivation.note: Scans through intervals that end before the new interval starts.
Scans and merges all intervals that overlap with the new interval.
Scans through any remaining intervals that come after the merge zone.

data.time_summary: Each element in the input array is visited at most a constant number of times across the three sequential while loops. The measured evidence confirms that step counts scale linearly (doubling n roughly doubles the total steps), resulting in O(n) total time complexity.
data.space_summary: We allocate a new result list to store the final output intervals. In the worst case, no intervals are merged and we store all n original intervals plus the new interval, requiring O(n) extra space.
data.takeaway: When working with sorted intervals, avoid sorting from scratch; instead, partition the input into three phases (before, during, and after the overlap) to process everything in a single linear pass.
mistakes: Failing to account for the edge case where the intervals list is completely empty.
Forgetting to append the merged new interval to the result list if it does not overlap with any existing intervals or if the list ends while merging.
Attempting to modify the input list in-place while iterating with indices, which leads to out-of-bounds errors or skipped elements.
